title: Ferguson? Guardiola? Mourinho? Ranking the best managers in Premier League history
description: ByAlex BysouthBBC Sport senior journalistWhen it comes to ranking managers, titles are a good place to start.Only four bosses have won more than one s
body: ByAlex BysouthBBC Sport senior journalistWhen it comes to ranking managers, titles are a good place to start.Only four bosses have won more than one since the Premier League era began in 1992. So if you do some quick maths, you'll probably not be surprised by the names that top this list.But there is a debate to be had around where they should rank, and who else makes it into the top 10. So let's have it.You can rank your greatest managers of the Premier League era below too.A question of longevity?Longevity deserves a mention here. Take David Moyes, for example, racking up 755 games in Premier League dugouts - only Arsene Wenger (828) and Sir Alex Ferguson (810) have more.Naturally, Moyes has the third-most wins in Premier League history too, although his 291 across spells with Everton, Manchester United, Sunderland and West Ham fall some way short of Wenger's 476 at Arsenal and Ferguson's 528 at United.Pep Guardiola is also on Scotsman Moyes' shoulder despite managing barely half as many games.Harry Redknapp has the fourth-most games under his belt (641), fifth-most wins (236) and also completes the top five for goals scored (818).We should talk about win percentage too, and the former Tottenham manager who really deserves a shout here is Mauricio Pochettino, who guided Spurs to their best-ever Premier League finish of second in 2016-17 and also coached Southampton and Chelsea.The Argentine is the only manager - of those who have coached more than 100 games - to have not lifted the title yet still won more than half his games throughout his Premier League career.But really, to make this list, you have to have won a Premier League title. In total, 13 managers have done so. Meaning three are getting left at the door.Arne Slot of Liverpool is the first to be cut. The others are a hard choice.Manuel Pellegrini's Manchester City record was impressive before the Chilean made way for Guardiola. During those three years, plus 17 months at West Ham, his average of 1.92 goals per game ranks fifth among all managers with a century of matches.But he spent big at the Hammers only to then endure a desperate run of form - so the man known as the Engineer, the only manager from outside Europe to win the title, misses out.As does Antonio Conte, who had boom and bust spells at Chelsea and Spurs.Instead, the pair are pipped by the only boss to win the title in all of Europe's top five leagues.10. Carlo Ancelotti. Title winner 2009-10AC Milan, Bayern Munich, Paris St-Germain, Real Madrid and, of course, Chelsea.King Carlo has steered them all to domestic glory, not to mention his Champions League record of five successes. Yet his initial tenure in the English top flight was fleeting.The Italian blitzed his way to the Premier League crown at the first time of asking at Stamford Bridge. But, after snapping up Fernando Torres for a then-British record fee from Liverpool the following January, Ancelotti was swiftly shown the door after Chelsea finished as runners-up in his second season.A surprising return to England came via the Everton dugout, where Ancelotti delivered successive mid-table finishes before Real Madrid came calling.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ancelotti's Chelsea thumped Wigan 8-0 to wrap up the title in 20109. Mikel Arteta. Title winner 2025-26Earlier this year, Mikel Arteta became the 13th manager to win the Premier League but the first Arsenal boss to do so since Arsene Wenger in 2004.The Spaniard also snapped an eight-year run of either Manchester City or Liverpool winning the trophy.Bursting clear of his rivals like they were a technical area, Arteta shrugged off questions over his team's sometimes robust style as well as those who suggested the Gunners were destined to always be runners-up.As the only current Premier League boss to have won the title, and with Arsenal adding to an already stacked squad this summer, you wouldn't bet against the former playmaker creeping further up this list in future.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mikel Arteta won his first Premier League title as a manager earlier this year8. Roberto Mancini. Title winner 2011-12Agueroooo! And all that.Premier League titles don't come more dramatic than two goals in added time - including a 94th-minute winner - on the final day of the season, especially to clinch a first top-flight crown in more than 40 years while denying your arch-rivals.Roberto Mancini got Manchester City's lavish new era rolling by winning the FA Cup in his first full season, having replaced Mark Hughes in December 2009, and followed up with the title before he was sacked the following summer.The Italian, though, stacks up well, boasting the fourth-best points-per-game tally for any boss to have managed at least 100 Premier League games - coming in just above Conte and Jose Mourinho - and the fifth-best win percentage.Meanwhile, his City stars make the top five for goals per game and boast the best record for fewest goals conceded, a miserly 0.83 per game.7. Kenny Dalglish. Title winner 1994-95Kenny Dalglish's greatest success as a boss came at Liverpool before the Premier League era began, winning three titles in four seasons, initially as a player-manager, before he departed in February 1991 after almost 15 years with the club.He wound up at second-tier Blackburn Rovers eight months later and immediately steered them into the Premier League via the play-offs.Bankrolled by local businessman Jack Walker, Rovers snapped up Alan Shearer from Southampton for a British record fee of £3.6m and then finished fourth and second before overcoming Manchester United to win the title in 1995.That made Dalglish only the fourth manager to win the English top flight with two different clubs.Dalglish was unable to repeat the trick at Newcastle, although they finished runners-up in both the league and FA Cup during his tenure, while his return to Liverpool ended in 2012 after League Cup success but an eighth-placed finish.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dalglish won top-flight titles at Liverpool and Blackburn6. Claudio Ranieri. Title winner 2015-16Dilly ding, dilly dong. Ranieri rides into the top six on pure vibes. The man behind the 5,000-1 miracle. The one who turned a cast of footballing misfits into an all-conquering force. The father of Leicester City's Premier League triumph.That is worth his entry alone. Yet, in what seems another lifetime, the Tinkerman almost got his hands on a winner's medal more than a decade earlier.Buoyed by the first wave of Roman Abramovich spending, Ranieri steered Chelsea to second in 2004, only behind Arsenal's Invincibles.Chelsea probably should have won the Champions League too, losing in the semi-finals to Monaco, but that became a defining moment for the man who would replace him.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Claudio Ranieri guided 5,000-1 shots Leicester to the Premier League title5. Jurgen Klopp. Title winner 2019-20Jurgen Klopp is in some ways the Andy Murray of the Premier League. All action, high-octane performances, adored by his fans yet prickly under pressure. He enjoyed incredible success but would probably have dominated more were it not for a generational opponent.In this rather stretched analogy, Manchester City are Klopp's Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic. If it had not been for his Catalan counterpart down the M62, Klopp's rock 'n' roll Reds would have been the undoubted top dogs under the German.Instead, they racked up more than 90 points on three occasions and 'only' clinched one title in 2019-20 - it was, however, Liverpool's first in 30 years and their first of the Premier League era.4. Jose Mourinho. Title winner 2004-05, 05-06 & 14-15Lungs still pumping from that touchline sprint at Old Trafford, Jose Mourinho landed at Chelsea days after guiding Porto to a remarkable Champions League triumph and declared himself a 'Special One'.Taking the baton from Ranieri and armed with a host of new signings, the Portuguese enigma stormed the title in his first season - Chelsea winning the league by 12 points, conceding only 15 goals and ruffling the raincoats of Wenger and Ferguson.Mourinho backed it up in his second season before relationships began to fray and the most successful boss in the club's history left in September 2007. Mourinho, though, had transformed the Blues into a formidable force.He returned six years later, after titles in Milan and Madrid, and clinched his third Premier League crown in his second season, only to be gone by Christmas of the following campaign.Box-office spells followed at Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur, but they came nowhere near the success of his time in south-west London.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jose Mourinho is one of only three managers to win successive Premier League titles - Sir Alex Ferguson won three in a row twice, while Pep Guardiola won four in a row3. Arsene Wenger. Title winner 1997-98, 2001-02 & 03-04It's fine margins between Wenger and Mourinho, as both their arrivals brought the dawn of new eras in the Premier League.Indeed, Mourinho once said Wenger is a "specialist in failure", but in this list the Frenchman just pips his rival thanks to engineering the only 'Invincibles' season in Premier League history.Wenger, joining from Japanese outfit Nagoya Grampus Eight, was deemed a curious choice at first but professionalised Arsenal and led them to league titles in 1998, 2002 and - the piece de resistance - that unbeaten season of 2003-04.That he was unable to win another title in the 14 years that followed perhaps tarnishes Wenger's legacy slightly, but the Arsenal team he built during his first decade was one of the best the Premier League ever witnessed.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Arsene Wenger won three Premier League titles with Arsenal - including the unbeaten season in 2003-042. Pep Guardiola. Title winner 2017-18, 18-19, 20-21, 21-22, 22-23 & 23-24Talking of managers who changed the face of English football, no-one has moved the game right from the elite level through to grassroots as much as Pep Guardiola.Blame the Catalan for Sunday League goalkeepers playing out from the back.And to think there were question marks over whether Guardiola's style - honed at Barcelona - would work in the more robust English game.Guardiola was, of course, lavishly backed in the transfer market, but his Manchester City side won titles at a prolific rate.City became the first English men's side to win four in a row - they landed six Premier League titles in total during Pep's decade in charge, as well as notching a century of points in 2018.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Guardiola won six titles before leaving Manchester City in the summer1. Sir Alex Ferguson. Title winner 1992-93, 93-94, 95-96, 96-97, 98-99, 99-2000, 2000-01, 02-03, 06-07, 07-08, 08-09, 10-11, 12-13The first two decades of the Premier League were dominated by one man.Sir Alex Ferguson won 13 titles and was able to continuously rebuild his side in order to keep Manchester United at the top of English football - from Eric Cantona to the '99 Treble winners, and later that front three of Cristiano Ronaldo, Wayne Rooney and Carlos Tevez.Even after Ronaldo left for Real Madrid in 2009, and Tevez defected to the other side of Manchester, Ferguson continued winning titles until he retired in 2013.His record title haul is more than double any manager from any era of men's English top-flight football, not just the Premier League - Guardiola, Liverpool's Bob Paisley and George Ramsay for Aston Villa are next on the list on six.It makes Fergie the undoubted number one.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ferguson won 13 Premier League titles with Manchester United

schema.headline: Ferguson? Guardiola? Mourinho? Ranking the best managers in Premier League history

title: UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources' says Kremlin advisor
description: Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to the Kremlin, says there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sha
body: Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to the Kremlin, says there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sharing of blueprints for British-made cruise missile components.His comments on BBC Newsnight come as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he plans to travel to the US next month with European leaders to lobby US President Trump on Ukraine's defence needs. He said that while the details were not "fully confirmed", it is "likely" he will go. The trip would be his first to the US since becoming prime minister in July. "Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks," he said following his official visit to Ukraine on Monday, during which he promised to continue pressuring Russia.The UK has also agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The blueprints will allow Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.Fedorov, who is Russia's former deputy foreign minister, said Putin was facing "serious" pressure "to undertake certain measures against UK". Asked on BBC Newsnight where the pressure was coming from, Fedorov responded, "public opinion polls, it's coming from journalists, from mass media". Asked what a "semi-military" response might look like, Fedorov said "it could take the form of something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine." "They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources," he said.The comments are in line with those made by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday, when he criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them."Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"Burnham's visit to Ukraine was his first official international visit. He met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. Burnham has been reaffirming the UK's support for Ukraine in the wake of escalating Russian strikes in recent weeks - including one last week on a shopping centre that killed at least 16 people.Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles, but stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.Zelensky has said he is hoping to secure 300 patriot missiles ahead of winter, when Russia is likely to increase its attacks on energy infrastructure, as it has done in past years. In the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said that he felt "really confident" that the issue was "fixable". But he pointed out that it wasn't only the US who could supply Ukraine with Patriots. "There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with," he said. "It's probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation."In July this year, three weeks after offering Ukraine the right to produce Patriots itself, Trump backtracked, saying, "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology."  "These weapons are incredible. We have to be very careful about letting somebody build them," Trump told a cabinet meeting. In a joint statement after the meeting in Ukraine, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority".They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the "shadow fleet".In a statement ahead of the visit, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes."I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."

schema.headline: UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources' says Kremlin advisor

title: HPV home-testing kits now available for women who have missed cervical screening
description: Gem Sofianos-Boorman, 39, said her experience shows how important the screening is. She was diagnosed with cervical cancer at 28, following screening,
body: Gem Sofianos-Boorman, 39, said her experience shows how important the screening is. She was diagnosed with cervical cancer at 28, following screening, and says it was the last thing she expected, given she was young, healthy and had no symptoms.She had surgery to remove the cancerous cells plus lymph nodes from her abdomen and pelvis to stop it spreading."Looking back, I truly believe that going to my screening appointment saved my life. My cancer was found early, which allowed me to have treatment before it spread."That's why it's great news that the NHS is making it more accessible for some people to take part in screening."Cervical cancer often doesn't cause any symptoms until the disease is more advanced and harder to treat."If you receive an invite to cervical screening, or an offer of a self-testing kit, please don't ignore it - it could save your life."Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women's health, said: "Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a game-changer – making it easier than ever for them to get tested."There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test."The kits contain a swab, similar to a long cotton, bud which is used to collect a sample from the vagina.It is then sent back to the NHS and if high-risk HPV is found, individuals will be invited to book a follow-up cervical screening appointment.High-risk HPV increases the risk of cervical cancer, but it does not mean a woman will automatically develop it.Trials of the self-testing in London suggest it could lead to one in 10 women to come forward for screening – boosting uptake by around 400,000 a year.Other parts of the UK are also looking at introducing self-testing.Women aged 24 to 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years – or more frequently if HPV is detected.Through a combination of HPV vaccination, which is offered to teenagers, and improved screening, the NHS is hoping to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040.The NHS says cervical screening appointments with a clinician is still the best way to prevent cancer – and even if you have missed an appointment you can still come forward for one.

schema.headline: HPV home-testing kits now available for women who have missed cervical screening
